Assignment 8 — Pneumonia Detection using a CNN¶

Goal: build a Convolutional Neural Network that classifies chest X-ray images as Pneumonia Positive or Pneumonia Negative (normal).

Dataset: Chest X-Ray Images (Pneumonia) on Kaggle (Kermany et al., Cell 2018). 5,856 paediatric chest X-rays (patients aged 1–5) from Guangzhou Women and Children's Medical Center, labelled by expert physicians.

Requirement Section
Download and organise the Kaggle Pneumonia Chest X-Ray dataset 1
Create our own CNN architecture 3
Apply Batch Normalization, Dropout and Data Augmentation 2.3, 3
Train the model and visualise accuracy and loss 4
Evaluate with a confusion matrix and suitable classification metrics 5

1. Download and organise the dataset¶

1.1 Download¶

The dataset (about 1.2 GB) is downloaded from Kaggle with the official kagglehub client into data/download/. If it is already there, the download is skipped.

In [3]:

1.2 Problems with the original split, and how I re-organise it¶

  1. The validation set has only 16 images (8 per class). Early stopping or model selection based on 16 images would be pure noise: one image is 6% accuracy.
  2. Several images per patient. File names carry a patient ID (e.g. person1000_bacteria_2931.jpeg, IM-0115-0001.jpeg), and the 3,875 training pneumonia images come from about 1,600 patients. If images were split at random, X-rays of the same child would land in both train and validation, and validation scores would be inflated by memorised patient-specific features.
  3. Class imbalance: about 74% of training images are pneumonia.

Re-organisation:

  • The original train and val images (5,232) are pooled and re-split into a new train (≈ 86%) and validation (≈ 14%) with StratifiedGroupKFold. The split is grouped by patient, so all of a patient's images land on the same side, and stratified by class, so both sides keep the same pneumonia ratio.
  • The official test set (624 images) is kept unchanged as the final hold-out, so results are comparable with other work on this dataset.
  • The result is written to data/chest_xray_organized/{train,val,test}/{NORMAL,PNEUMONIA}/ using hard links, which gives a clean folder structure without using extra disk space. A manifest.csv records every file's split, label and patient ID.
  • The imbalance is handled with class weights during training (Section 4).
In [4]:
def patient_id(fname: str) -> str:
    """'person1000_bacteria_2931.jpeg' -> 'person1000' | 'NORMAL2-IM-1427-0001.jpeg' -> 'NORMAL2-IM-1427'."""
    m = re.match(r"(person\d+)_", fname)
    return m.group(1) if m else re.sub(r"-\d+\.jpeg$", "", fname)

rows = []
for split in ["train", "val", "test"]:
    for label, cls in enumerate(CLASSES):
        for f in sorted((RAW / split / cls).glob("*.jpeg")):
            rows.append({"src": str(f), "file": f.name, "orig_split": split, "cls": cls, "label": label,
                         "patient": f"{cls[0]}-{patient_id(f.name)}"})
manifest = pd.DataFrame(rows)

dev = manifest[manifest.orig_split != "test"].copy()
sgkf = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=7, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
_, val_idx = next(sgkf.split(dev, dev["label"], groups=dev["patient"]))
dev["split"] = "train"
dev.iloc[val_idx, dev.columns.get_loc("split")] = "val"
manifest = pd.concat([dev, manifest[manifest.orig_split == "test"].assign(split="test")], ignore_index=True)

overlap = set(manifest.query("split == 'train'").patient) & set(manifest.query("split == 'val'").patient)
print(f"patients shared between new train and val: {len(overlap)}")
print(f"images: {len(manifest):,} | unique patients in train+val: {dev.patient.nunique():,}")

ORG = DATA_DIR / "chest_xray_organized"
if ORG.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(ORG)
for r in manifest.itertuples():
    dst = ORG / r.split / r.cls / r.file
    dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        os.link(r.src, dst)                           # hard link: no extra disk space
    except OSError:
        shutil.copy2(r.src, dst)
manifest["path"] = [str(ORG / s / c / f) for s, c, f in zip(manifest.split, manifest["cls"], manifest.file)]
manifest.drop(columns="src").to_csv(DATA_DIR / "manifest.csv", index=False)

split_counts = manifest.pivot_table(index="split", columns="cls", values="file", aggfunc="count").loc[["train", "val", "test"]]
split_counts["total"] = split_counts.sum(axis=1)
split_counts["% pneumonia"] = (split_counts["PNEUMONIA"] / split_counts["total"] * 100).round(1)
split_counts["patients"] = manifest.groupby("split")["patient"].nunique()

Normal lungs look dark (air-filled) with sharp outlines. Pneumonia shows hazy white opacities (fluid or infiltrates). Bacterial pneumonia tends to be focal (lobar consolidation), while viral pneumonia is more diffuse. The images vary widely in size and aspect ratio, so they are all resized to a common input size.

2. Input pipeline¶

2.1 Loading¶

  • Images are read as grayscale (1 channel). X-rays carry no colour information, so 3 RGB channels would triple memory and computation for nothing.
  • Every image is resized to 160 × 160. That is enough resolution to see opacities, and small enough to train a CNN from scratch on a laptop CPU in reasonable time.
  • After the first pass, decoded images are cached in memory so later epochs skip the costly JPEG decoding.
In [7]:
def make_dataset(split, training):
    df = manifest[manifest.split == split]
    ds = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((df["path"].values, df["label"].values.astype("float32")))

    def load(path, label):
        img = tf.io.decode_jpeg(tf.io.read_file(path), channels=1)
        img = tf.image.resize(img, (IMG_SIZE, IMG_SIZE), antialias=True)
        return tf.cast(tf.round(img), tf.uint8), label            # uint8 keeps the in-memory cache small

    ds = ds.map(load, num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE).cache()
    if training:
        ds = ds.shuffle(len(df), seed=SEED, reshuffle_each_iteration=True)
    return ds.map(lambda x, y: (tf.cast(x, tf.float32), y)).batch(BATCH).prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)

train_ds, val_ds, test_ds = make_dataset("train", True), make_dataset("val", False), make_dataset("test", False)
y_train = manifest.query("split == 'train'")["label"].values
y_val = manifest.query("split == 'val'")["label"].values
y_test = manifest.query("split == 'test'")["label"].values

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in train_ds: pass                                 # warm the cache once (decodes every JPEG)
for _ in val_ds: pass
for _ in test_ds: pass
print(f"decoded and cached {len(manifest):,} images in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f}s")

decoded and cached 5,856 images in 4s

2.2 Class weights¶

With about 74% pneumonia in the training set, a network could reach 74% accuracy by always answering "pneumonia". Class weights scale each sample's loss contribution inversely to its class frequency, so the rarer NORMAL class counts proportionally more and both classes contribute equally to the total loss:

In [8]:
n, n_pos = len(y_train), int(y_train.sum())
class_weight = {0: n / (2 * (n - n_pos)), 1: n / (2 * n_pos)}
print({CLASSES[k]: round(v, 3) for k, v in class_weight.items()})

{'NORMAL': 1.939, 'PNEUMONIA': 0.674}

2.3 Data augmentation¶

Augmentation creates random, label-preserving variations of each training image on the fly, so the network never sees exactly the same picture twice. It acts as a regularizer and teaches invariance to irrelevant changes in patient positioning and exposure.

Transformation Setting Real-world variation it simulates
RandomRotation ± 5% of a full turn (≈ ±18°) a patient not perfectly upright
RandomZoom ± 10% different distance to the detector
RandomTranslation ± 8% horizontally and vertically off-centre positioning
RandomContrast ± 15% different exposure settings and machines

Horizontal flips are deliberately not used. Chest anatomy is asymmetric (the heart sits on the left), so a mirrored X-ray is not a realistic image.

The augmentation layers are part of the model. Keras applies them only during training, and they are inactive during validation, testing and inference.

In [9]:
augmentation = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.RandomRotation(0.05, fill_mode="constant", fill_value=0.0),
    keras.layers.RandomZoom(0.10, fill_mode="constant", fill_value=0.0),
    keras.layers.RandomTranslation(0.08, 0.08, fill_mode="constant", fill_value=0.0),
    keras.layers.RandomContrast(0.15, value_range=(0, 255)),
], name="augmentation")

example = next(iter(train_ds.unbatch().batch(1)))[0]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(15, 2.9))
axes[0].imshow(example[0, ..., 0], cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255); axes[0].set_title("original")
for i, ax in enumerate(axes[1:], start=1):
    aug = augmentation(example, training=True)
    ax.imshow(np.clip(aug[0, ..., 0], 0, 255), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255); ax.set_title(f"augmented #{i}")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout(); save(fig, "03_augmentation_examples")

3. CNN architecture (built from scratch)¶

Input 160×160×1 ─► Augmentation (train only) ─► Rescaling to [0, 1]
  Block 1:  Conv 3×3, 32  ─► BatchNorm ─► ReLU ─► MaxPool 2×2                       → 80×80×32
  Block 2:  Conv 3×3, 64  ─► BatchNorm ─► ReLU ─► MaxPool 2×2                       → 40×40×64
  Block 3: [Conv 3×3, 128 ─► BatchNorm ─► ReLU] × 2 ─► MaxPool 2×2                  → 20×20×128
  Block 4: [Conv 3×3, 256 ─► BatchNorm ─► ReLU] × 2 ─► MaxPool 2×2                  → 10×10×256
  Global Average Pooling ─► Dropout 0.5 ─► Dense 128 + ReLU ─► Dropout 0.3 ─► Dense 1 + sigmoid

Design decisions

  • Convolution blocks with increasing filter counts (32 → 256), spatial size halved by max-pooling. Early layers detect edges and textures. Deeper layers combine them into larger patterns such as rib outlines, lung borders and opacity regions. Pooling grows the receptive field and adds some translation invariance.
  • Two convolutions in the deeper blocks give more non-linearity and a larger receptive field (two stacked 3×3 convolutions see 5×5) where the feature maps are small and cheap.
  • Batch Normalization after every convolution normalises the activations of each mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, then rescales them with learnable parameters. It stabilises and speeds up training (it allows a higher learning rate) and has a mild regularising effect. The convolutions therefore use use_bias=False, because BN's shift makes a bias redundant.
  • Global Average Pooling instead of Flatten: it averages each of the 256 final feature maps to one number. Flattening 10×10×256 into a dense layer would add about 3.3 M parameters; GAP keeps the head small and reduces overfitting.
  • Dropout (0.5 before and 0.3 after the dense layer) randomly zeroes activations during training, so the classifier cannot rely on any single feature. Like augmentation, it is turned off at inference time.
  • Sigmoid output gives P(pneumonia), trained with binary cross-entropy.
In [10]:
L = keras.layers

def conv_bn_relu(x, filters, name):
    x = L.Conv2D(filters, 3, padding="same", use_bias=False, kernel_initializer="he_normal", name=f"{name}_conv")(x)
    x = L.BatchNormalization(name=f"{name}_bn")(x)
    return L.Activation("relu", name=f"{name}_relu")(x)

def build_cnn():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(IMG_SIZE, IMG_SIZE, 1), name="xray")
    x = augmentation(inputs)
    x = L.Rescaling(1.0 / 255, name="rescale")(x)
    for b, (filters, n_conv) in enumerate([(32, 1), (64, 1), (128, 2), (256, 2)], start=1):
        for c in range(1, n_conv + 1):
            x = conv_bn_relu(x, filters, f"block{b}_{c}")
        x = L.MaxPooling2D(2, name=f"block{b}_pool")(x)
    x = L.GlobalAveragePooling2D(name="gap")(x)
    x = L.Dropout(0.5, name="dropout_1")(x)
    x = L.Dense(128, activation="relu", name="dense")(x)
    x = L.Dropout(0.3, name="dropout_2")(x)
    outputs = L.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="p_pneumonia")(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="pneumonia_cnn")

model = build_cnn()
model.summary(line_length=100)

4. Training¶

  • Optimizer: Adam, initial learning rate 0.0003. A first run with 0.001 had large validation-loss jumps from epoch to epoch, triggered early stopping at epoch 10 and reached a best validation loss of only 0.117. With 0.0003 training is slower but steadier and reaches a best validation loss of 0.068. Both choices were compared on the validation set only.
  • Loss: binary cross-entropy, with the class weights from Section 2.2.
  • Callbacks:
    • ReduceLROnPlateau halves the learning rate when validation loss stalls for 3 epochs, so the model can settle into a finer minimum;
    • EarlyStopping stops when validation loss has not improved for 8 epochs and restores the best weights;
    • ModelCheckpoint saves the best model to models/pneumonia_cnn.keras.
  • Up to 30 epochs. Validation uses the patient-grouped validation set (about 740 images), never the test set.
In [11]:
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=3e-4), loss="binary_crossentropy",
              metrics=["accuracy", keras.metrics.AUC(name="auc"),
                       keras.metrics.Precision(name="precision"), keras.metrics.Recall(name="recall")])
callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=3, min_lr=1e-5, verbose=1),
    keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=8, restore_best_weights=True, verbose=1),
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(MODEL_DIR / "pneumonia_cnn.keras", monitor="val_loss", save_best_only=True),
]
t0 = time.perf_counter()
history = model.fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, epochs=30, class_weight=class_weight,
                    callbacks=callbacks, shuffle=False,   # train_ds already reshuffles every epoch
                    verbose=2)
train_minutes = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 60
hist = pd.DataFrame(history.history, index=pd.RangeIndex(1, len(history.history["loss"]) + 1, name="epoch"))
hist.to_csv(RES_DIR / "training_history.csv")
best_epoch = int(hist["val_loss"].idxmin())
print(f"\ntrained {len(hist)} epochs in {train_minutes:.1f} min | best epoch (lowest val loss): {best_epoch}")

Reading the curves

  • Training loss falls steadily from 0.36 to about 0.07 and training accuracy rises to about 97%, so the network learns the task without trouble.
  • No serious overfitting. At most epochs validation tracks training closely. At the best epoch (15) the validation loss is 0.068, validation accuracy 97.2% and validation ROC-AUC 0.997, against a training loss of 0.094. Training metrics are computed with augmentation and dropout switched on, which is why they can sit slightly below the validation metrics.
  • Isolated validation spikes (epochs 7, 10 and 16): validation accuracy and recall drop sharply for one epoch, while validation ROC-AUC stays above 0.95. The ranking of the images is still good, and what moves is the calibration: for that epoch the network outputs lower pneumonia probabilities, so many pneumonia images fall below 0.5. This is common for CNNs trained from scratch with Batch Normalization, which uses batch statistics during training but running averages at inference, and class weights shift the boundary further. The next epoch recovers every time.
  • ReduceLROnPlateau halved the learning rate at epochs 13, 19 and 22 (marked "LR ↓"). Training loss kept falling but validation loss never beat epoch 15, so EarlyStopping ended training at epoch 23 and restored the weights of epoch 15. The last epoch is worse than the best one, which is exactly why the best weights are restored.

5. Evaluation on the held-out test set¶

5.1 Choosing the decision threshold¶

The network outputs P(pneumonia). The default rule "pneumonia if P ≥ 0.5" is not necessarily the best operating point, so I also pick the threshold that maximises Youden's J = sensitivity + specificity − 1 on the validation set. The test set is not used for this choice.

In [13]:

test_proba = model.predict(test_ds, verbose=0).ravel()
fpr_v, tpr_v, thr_v = roc_curve(y_val, val_proba)
best_thr = float(thr_v[np.argmax(tpr_v - fpr_v)])
print(f"validation ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y_val, val_proba):.4f} | Youden-optimal threshold on validation: {best_thr:.3f}")

validation ROC-AUC 0.9965 | Youden-optimal threshold on validation: 0.613

5.2 Metrics¶

Positive class = PNEUMONIA.

Metric Meaning in this application
Accuracy share of all X-rays classified correctly
Recall / sensitivity share of pneumonia cases that are detected. A miss (FN) means a sick child goes untreated, so this is the most important clinical metric
Specificity share of healthy children correctly cleared. Low specificity means unnecessary treatment and follow-up
Precision (PPV) when the model says "pneumonia", how often it is right
F1 score harmonic mean of precision and recall
ROC-AUC ranking quality across all thresholds (0.5 is random, 1 is perfect)
PR-AUC area under the precision-recall curve
In [14]:
def evaluate(y, proba, thr):
    pred = (proba >= thr).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y, pred).ravel()
    return {"threshold": thr, "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y, pred), "Recall (sensitivity)": recall_score(y, pred),
            "Specificity": tn / (tn + fp), "Precision": precision_score(y, pred), "F1": f1_score(y, pred),
            "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y, proba), "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(y, proba),
            "TP": tp, "FN": fn, "TN": tn, "FP": fp}

results = pd.DataFrame({"threshold 0.50": evaluate(y_test, test_proba, 0.5),
                        f"threshold {best_thr:.3f} (Youden, from val)": evaluate(y_test, test_proba, best_thr)}).T
results.to_csv(RES_DIR / "test_metrics.csv")
results.round(4)

5.3 Error analysis: what does the model get wrong?¶

In [17]:
test_df = manifest[manifest.split == "test"].reset_index(drop=True).assign(p=test_proba)
fp_ = test_df[(test_df.label == 0) & (test_df.p >= best_thr)].sort_values("p", ascending=False).head(5)
fn_ = test_df[(test_df.label == 1) & (test_df.p < best_thr)].sort_values("p").head(5)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(15, 6.4))
for row_axes, subset, title in [(axes[0], fp_, "False positive (true NORMAL)"), (axes[1], fn_, "False negative (true PNEUMONIA)")]:
    for ax in row_axes:
        ax.axis("off")
    for ax, r in zip(row_axes, subset.itertuples()):
        img = tf.io.decode_jpeg(tf.io.read_file(r.path), channels=1).numpy().squeeze()
        ax.imshow(img, cmap="gray"); ax.set_title(f"{title}\nP(pneumonia) = {r.p:.2f}", fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle("Most confident mistakes on the test set", fontweight="bold", color=INK)
fig.tight_layout(); save(fig, "07_misclassified_examples")

Observations

  • The errors are very lopsided. At the chosen threshold there are 80 false positives but only 3 false negatives: the model almost never misses pneumonia, but it flags about a third of the healthy children in the test set.
  • In the score histogram (Section 5.2) almost every pneumonia image gets P > 0.95. The scores of normal images are spread over the whole range, and a group of about 35 normal images gets P ≈ 1, so no threshold can separate those from pneumonia.
  • The most confident false positives are mostly hazy, low-contrast or slightly rotated exposures, where normal vessel markings can look like infiltrates to the network.
  • The three missed pneumonia cases have P between 0.21 and 0.32. The model was uncertain rather than confidently wrong. One of them is an A-P image with ECG electrodes on the chest, which is rare in the training data.

5.4 Where does the CNN look? (Grad-CAM)¶

Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017) highlights the image regions that most increased the pneumonia score. It takes the gradient of the output with respect to the last convolutional feature maps, averages it into one weight per channel, and uses those weights to combine the maps into a heat map. It is a sanity check that the network bases its decision on the lungs rather than on artefacts such as text markers or borders.

In [18]:
last_conv = "block4_2_relu"
grad_model = keras.Model(model.inputs, [model.get_layer(last_conv).output, model.output])

def grad_cam(img):
    x = tf.convert_to_tensor(img[None, ..., None], dtype=tf.float32)
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        fmap, pred = grad_model(x, training=False)
        score = pred[:, 0]
    grads = tape.gradient(score, fmap)
    weights = tf.reduce_mean(grads, axis=(0, 1, 2))
    cam = tf.nn.relu(tf.reduce_sum(fmap[0] * weights, axis=-1)).numpy()
    cam = cam / (cam.max() + 1e-8)
    return tf.image.resize(cam[..., None], (IMG_SIZE, IMG_SIZE)).numpy().squeeze(), float(pred[0, 0])

tp_examples = test_df[(test_df.label == 1) & (test_df.p >= best_thr)].sample(4, random_state=SEED)
tn_examples = test_df[(test_df.label == 0) & (test_df.p < best_thr)].sample(2, random_state=SEED)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(16, 6))
for k, r in enumerate(pd.concat([tp_examples, tn_examples]).itertuples()):
    img = tf.image.resize(tf.io.decode_jpeg(tf.io.read_file(r.path), channels=1), (IMG_SIZE, IMG_SIZE), antialias=True).numpy().squeeze()
    cam, p_ = grad_cam(img)
    axes[0, k].imshow(img, cmap="gray"); axes[0, k].set_title(f"{r.cls}, P = {p_:.2f}", fontsize=9)
    axes[1, k].imshow(img, cmap="gray"); axes[1, k].imshow(cam, cmap="inferno", alpha=0.45)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("X-ray", fontsize=10); axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Grad-CAM", fontsize=10)
fig.suptitle("Grad-CAM: regions driving the pneumonia score (4 detected pneumonia cases, 2 normal)",
             fontweight="bold", color=INK)
fig.tight_layout(); save(fig, "08_grad_cam")

Observations

  • For the detected pneumonia cases the heat maps lie on the lung fields, mainly the perihilar and lower zones where the opacities are, and not on the "R" side markers, text labels or image borders. The network is using clinically relevant regions.
  • The maps are coarse, because they are computed on the 10 × 10 output of the last convolution block and up-sampled to 160 × 160. They show regions, not exact lesion boundaries.
  • Some heat also falls on the heart and mediastinum, and for the second normal image (P = 0.34) partly on the shoulder near the top-left corner. This is a reminder that a CNN trained on one hospital's data can also pick up non-lung cues: Grad-CAM is a sanity check, not a proof that the model reasons like a radiologist.

6. Conclusion¶

Final model: our own 4-block CNN (about 1.16 M parameters, trained from scratch) with Batch Normalization after every convolution, Dropout 0.5 / 0.3 in the head and on-the-fly data augmentation. It trained in about 37 minutes on a laptop CPU (best epoch 15 of 23).

Test-set results (624 unseen images, decision threshold 0.613 chosen on the validation set):

Metric Value
Accuracy 86.7%
Recall / sensitivity 99.2% (387 of 390 pneumonia cases detected)
Specificity 65.8% (154 of 234 normal cases cleared)
Precision 82.9%
F1 score 0.903
ROC-AUC 0.958
PR-AUC 0.969

Discussion

  1. Very high sensitivity. Only 3 of 390 pneumonia cases were missed. For a screening aid this is the most important property, because a missed pneumonia is far more harmful than an extra check.
  2. The weak point is specificity. 80 of 234 healthy children were flagged as pneumonia. In practice these cases would get a second look from a radiologist, so the model reduces workload, but it cannot replace one.
  3. Validation vs test gap. Validation accuracy is 97.2% but test accuracy is 86.7%. Because the validation split is grouped by patient, this is not leakage. The official test set simply differs from the training data: its class balance is different (62.5% vs 74% pneumonia), and the normal test images get much more spread-out scores (validation ROC-AUC 0.997 vs test 0.958). This kind of distribution shift is the main reason models trained on this dataset score lower on its test set.
  4. Threshold tuning helped. Moving the threshold from 0.5 to the validation-optimal 0.613 increased test accuracy by 2.4 points and specificity by 6.4 points without losing any recall. The test ROC-AUC of 0.958 shows the model ranks images well. A threshold picked on the test set would score higher, but that would be cheating, so it is not done.
  5. Regularisation worked as intended. Augmentation, dropout and Batch Normalization kept the training and validation curves close together (no overfitting), and early stopping with best-weight restoration protected the model from the noisy validation epochs.

Possible improvements: a larger input size (224 px or more) to keep fine texture; more diverse training data from other hospitals, to reduce the distribution shift; probability calibration (for example temperature scaling) on data closer to deployment; test-time augmentation and an ensemble of models from several cross-validation folds; and, outside the "own architecture" scope of this assignment, transfer learning from a network pre-trained on large chest X-ray collections.

This is an educational project and not a medical device. It must not be used for clinical decisions.
